newsitem.title: UK: EMU seen as key to European share growth.
newsitem.headline: EMU seen as key to European share growth.

text.p: The introduction of a single European currency will herald a dramatic rise in the level and value of share dealings throughout Europe, according to academics, bourse officials and fund managers.

They say the "euro", set for launch in 1999, should be the driving force behind the harmonisation and enhancement of cross-border EU share trading. But it will take time before monetary union makes equities more attractive.

"Monetary union will act as a far more powerful force for liberalising European market structure than any directive or piece of legislation ever could," said Dr. Benn Steil, chief economist at the Royal Institute of International Affairs.

Steil believes that without a single currency, institutional investors afraid of seeing the value of their shares fall due to an unattractive exchange rate, tend to adopt an investment bias toward their own domestic listed shares.
A single currency will not only increase cross-border turnover but will fundamentally change the structure of equities dealings in Europe, Steil said.

"After the currency risk is removed, domestic exchanges and electronic dealing systems throughout Europe will have to compete against each other head-on with virtually nothing to distinguish them," he said.
Steil's view, based on a 12-month study of the structure of European bourses, is shared by the chairman of the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, Boudewijn Van Ittersun.
"It will increase cross-border investment and there is no doubt about it," Van Ittersun said.
He said Dutch shares are popular amongst international investors but the lack of a single currency is still a major deterrent for many foreign institutions.

"We have the disadvantage today in Holland where we have a strong economy but a small-based currency, which limits the potential for investors -- they like our economy but they don't like the currency risk," he said.
A major fund manager is also looking forward to the introduction of the euro.

Kees van Rees, managing director of Shell Pension Fund Management in Amsterdam noted that his pension fund had lost heavily due to currency exposure over the last few years adding that "last year alone we lost well over 2.5 percent on currencies ".
"The currency is the important factor," he said. DRAMATIC NEAR-TERM IMPACT UNLIKELY
Although the euro has its supporters, its introduction will not necessarily in itself, guarantee any near-term jump in European share trading, strategists said.
Market professionals believe that existing fundamental financial structures across Europe will continue to inhibit institutional investors from any dramatic change in cross-border asset allocations.

"The single currency will not solve some of the underlying problems such as accounting differences and different valuation parameters that are used throughout Europe," said Andy Hartwill, equities strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Hartwill said stockbrokers throughout the EU had for many years been offering advice to institutions looking to invest in a wide variety of shares throughout Europe -- but with only limited success.
"This pan-European sector approach has been going on long before there was talk of a single currency," Hartwill said.
"We have been confronted daily by complicated calculations on valuations."

The EU's Investment Services Directive(ISD), which took effect last January is supposed to be the pass key that will allow share brokers and stock exchanges in the EU to unlock investor capital which has, until recently, been trapped behind these structural differences.

Although the ISD does allow banks and brokers to operate throughout the EU with virtually the same freedom they enjoy in their home markets, it has not yet addressed suchs problems as diverse accounting practices or taxation differences. PENSION FUND REGULATIONS DIFFER
In additiion, equity holdings of EU pension funds, both domestic and cross-border, are strongly influenced by regulations such as those relating to minimum funding and portfolio composition.

French institutional investors, for example, are being forced to help fund France's huge budget deficit by heavily investing in domestic government bonds, according to the head of the French insurance trade association.

"Yes, we are funding the budget deficit," said Denis Kessler, President of the Federation Francaise des Societes d'Assurances (FSSA). In 1995, the French government's deficit was FF323 billion and the 1996 deficit is projected to be FF289.7 billion.

At present, private pension funds are banned in France but a bill has been introduced in the National Assembly which will allow such funds. If the bill is passed, private pension funds will be able to invest a maximum of 65 percent in bonds, leaving the way open for hefty investment in equities.

France's stock market association (SBF) believes the introduction of private pensions will generate big flows into shares. "There will be a natural flow of investment into shares, which offer higher long-term returns," an SBF spokesman said.
Although private pensions in France will free up some capital, asset allocation, particularly in continental Europe, is unlikely to be immediately influenced by a single currency, Hartwill said.
